content: A stillbirth occurs when a fetus that was expected to survive dies either during the process of birth or in the latter half of pregnancy. Causes of Stillbirth: Stillbirth may result from a variety of factors, including: Congenital birth defects. Chromosomal abnormalities. Infections affecting either the mother or the fetus. Physical injuries. Maternal medical conditions such as diabetes, epilepsy, or hypertension. Placental complications, such as placental abruption or inadequate placental function. Sudden and severe maternal or fetal blood loss (hemorrhage). Cardiac arrest in either the mother or the fetus, leading to cessation of the heartbeat. Issues with the umbilical cord. In approximately 15–35% of stillbirth cases, no definitive cause can be identified. Diagnosis: The incidence of stillbirth has been decreasing due to advancements in prenatal care. If a stillbirth occurs, healthcare providers may request to conduct a thorough examination and testing of the fetus to identify the underlying cause. This information can be valuable for planning medical care in future pregnancies. A complete autopsy of the fetus will typically be offered to the parents. However, parents have the option to decline this procedure if they choose. Prognosis and Emotional Impact: Experiencing a stillbirth is a profoundly traumatic event for the mother and her family. It often leads to intense grief and may increase the risk of postpartum depression.
